passage:
Monday. In the back of his rough notebook, Lokesh, ten, kept a list: Baljeet lent eraser (2 times). Me helped Baljeet with maps (1). Ritu owes me a pencil.
Wednesday. After the class clean-up, Sir handed out laddoos: three for Lokesh, "my best helper", and one for Baljeet. Lokesh's face went red. "That's not fair! Baljeet carried six chairs, I carried four. He should get more!" The class stared. Sir blinked. "Lokesh, it's a laddoo." "It's the rule," Lokesh said, and pushed one across the desk.
Saturday. Baljeet saw the list while copying homework. "You count everything?" Lokesh shrugged, cheeks hot. "Someone has to." Baljeet laughed and crossed out "eraser (2)". "Keep your list. I don't need a bill."

qa.q: How many chairs did Baljeet carry, according to Lokesh?
qa.a: Lokesh said Baljeet carried six chairs and Lokesh carried four.

qa.q: Why did Lokesh's face go red when he got three laddoos?
qa.a: He felt upset that the split was unfair by his count, since Baljeet had worked harder, even though he was the one getting extra.

qa.q: Lokesh pushed a laddoo across. What could he try next time a split feels wrong?
qa.a: He could raise it quietly with Sir instead of shouting it in front of the class, keeping the fairness without the scene.

qa.q: How might Baljeet feel on finding himself listed in Lokesh's notebook?
qa.a: Baljeet seems amused rather than hurt, and wants to show Lokesh that their friendship doesn't need keeping count.

grounding: Across a week, a child keeps a tally of favours and loudly objects to a split that favours himself, showing an early, rigid sense of fairness.

passage: Jomon, you're counting the chocolates again, I can see your lips moving. Come here, mone. When your Seema aunty was nine, I was worse. I kept a tally on the kitchen wall with charcoal: who pumped water, who fed the hens, who helped whom with sums. One day my father cut a jackfruit and gave me the biggest share because I had swept the yard. I shouted, "No! Thomas pumped water twice, he gets more!" Everyone laughed, and my father said, "Seema, just eat." I wouldn't touch it until Thomas had the bigger piece. I was right about fairness, mind you. But I was so busy counting that I never enjoyed a single bite. Share them, mone, and don't keep a wall.

qa.q: Where did young Seema keep her tally?
qa.a: On the kitchen wall, with charcoal.

qa.q: Why wouldn't young Seema touch her jackfruit?
qa.a: She felt the split was unfair because Thomas had pumped water twice, and she couldn't enjoy extra she felt she hadn't earned.

qa.q: What is Seema aunty hoping Jomon will choose with the chocolates?
qa.a: She hopes Jomon will share them freely rather than counting every piece, keeping fairness without letting the tally spoil the fun.

qa.q: How might Thomas have felt when young Seema shouted that he should get more?
qa.a: Thomas may have been surprised and a bit embarrassed by the fuss, but perhaps pleased that his work was noticed.

grounding: An elder recalls how, as a child, she kept a tally of chores and refused a bigger share that was meant for her, fairness held rigidly.

passage: The school fair closed in five minutes, the lights were going off one by one, and the lemonade stall's tin was full of sticky coins. "Quick, just grab and go," said Pallavi, pushing a bigger heap towards Himani. "You made the sign." "No!" Himani's voice rang across the ground. "You squeezed forty lemons. I only squeezed twelve. And Mehak washed all the cups. We count it properly." The watchman was already rattling his keys at the gate. Pallavi groaned. Himani knelt on the grass, sorting coins by torchlight: one pile for squeezing, one for cups, one for the sign. Her own pile came out smallest. She nodded, satisfied, just as the gate clanged.

qa.q: How many lemons did Pallavi squeeze, according to Himani?
qa.a: Himani said Pallavi squeezed forty lemons.

qa.q: Why did Himani look satisfied even though her own pile came out smallest?
qa.a: What mattered to her was that each pile matched the work done; a fair count felt better than extra coins.

qa.q: With the gate closing, what could Himani have chosen instead of sorting every coin?
qa.a: She could have taken the tin home and split it properly next day, keeping fairness without keeping everyone waiting in the dark.

qa.q: What is it like for Pallavi to have a generous offer turned down so loudly?
qa.a: Pallavi may feel frustrated and a little embarrassed, since the bigger heap was meant kindly and she just wanted to go home.

grounding: A child insists loudly on an exact split of stall money by effort, even though it leaves her with less, showing a rigid sense of fairness.

passage: Minakshi, nine, and Hafsa washed Mr Kapoor's car every Sunday in their Lucknow colony. This Sunday, Mr Kapoor gave Minakshi sixty rupees and Hafsa forty. "For my neighbour's girl, a little extra," he winked. Minakshi's face went hot. "That's not fair! Hafsa did the wheels and the mats. I only did the windows. She should get more!" Mr Kapoor laughed. "It's only twenty rupees, beta." "It's the rule," Minakshi said, and pushed twenty rupees into Hafsa's hand. That night she opened her notebook. Every Sunday had a line: who did wheels, who did windows, who brought the bucket. Hafsa, reading over her shoulder, giggled. "You even wrote the bucket?" "Somebody has to keep it fair," Minakshi said, underlining it twice.

qa.q: How much money did Mr Kapoor first give Minakshi?
qa.a: He gave Minakshi sixty rupees.

qa.q: Why was Minakshi upset even though she got more money?
qa.a: She felt the split was unfair because Hafsa had done the wheels and the mats, which was more work than her windows.

qa.q: What does Minakshi's notebook do well, and where could it go too far?
qa.a: It helps her keep things fair, but counting even the bucket every week could turn a fun friendship into a strict account.

qa.q: How does Hafsa see Minakshi's notebook?
qa.a: Hafsa finds it funny that her friend writes down even who brought the bucket, though she also benefits from Minakshi's sense of fairness.

grounding: A nine-year-old refuses an unequal payment in her favour and keeps a strict notebook of who did what, showing an emerging, rigid sense of fairness.

passage:
"Nani, you gave me thirty and Nikhil twenty." Ankita, ten, held up the coins.
"You fetched the vegetables, beti."
"But Nikhil fetched the milk twice and the newspaper. That's three trips. I only did one."
Nikhil, eight, looked up hopefully. "She's right, Nani."
"Arrey, it's just pocket money."
"It's not fair if it's not counted." Ankita took out a sheet of paper. "I'm making a chart. Trips, sweeping, watering plants. Each gets five rupees."
"And who checks the chart?" Nani asked, amused.
"Me."
"And if I give you extra because you're my first grandchild?"
"Then I'll give it to Nikhil." Ankita slid ten rupees across the table.
Nani shook her head, smiling. "This girl will run a bank one day."
Nikhil pocketed the coins before anyone could change their mind.

qa.q: What did Ankita fetch for Nani?
qa.a: She fetched the vegetables.

qa.q: What does Ankita's chart suggest about how she feels about fairness?
qa.a: It suggests she is determined that fairness means counting exactly, even when counting leaves her with less.

qa.q: How could Nani help Ankita keep fairness without making it rigid?
qa.a: She could praise Ankita's honesty and also explain that small gifts of love don't always need to be counted like payments.

qa.q: How does Nikhil see Ankita's rule?
qa.a: Nikhil is happy and a bit surprised, since Ankita's strict counting gives Nikhil more money.

grounding: A ten-year-old objects to an unequal split in her favour and makes a strict chart of chores, showing a strong but rigid sense of fairness.
